SABA 2.0 is scaling to 50,000 healthy adults in Sardinia's Blue Zone, with continuous wearables joined to clinical events. The science of healthspan and longevity behind Nuraxi.
SABA 2.0: scaling to 50,000 healthy adults, continuous wearables, clinical events. The measurement medicine never made.
Research: SABA 2.0 and the science of staying well | Nuraxi Skip to content Demo Menu Home Solutions Use cases Research Request a demo Log in Portal Sign out Research The science of staying well. Medicine studies the ill, so it understands illness. Longevity has the opposite problem: the decades a healthy body spends staying well have never been measured at scale. Our research program exists to make that measurement. The thesis You cannot compress what you do not count. The world lives about a decade longer than it lives well: a 9.6-year mean gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy across 183 WHO member states, and it has been widening. We think that is a measurement failure before it is a treatment failure. Healthspan The years lived in function. The word exists, and it moved the field. Morbispan The expected years a person will live with chronic disease. We propose the word, because the sector optimises what it names: a personal number, forecast with a confidence interval, updated as you live. Reference ranges come from convenience samples of the "apparently healthy." Biobanks enrol the unusually well: UK Biobank volunteers in their early seventies show all-cause mortality roughly half that of the general population (Fry et al., American Journal of Epidemiology, 2017). And the clinical record starts at diagnosis. Between the sick record and the volunteer cohort sits the actual population, described by neither. Wearables were supposed to fix this, and they carry staggering volume: millions of samples per person per day. But a wearable never learns what happened to its wearer. The signal has no outcomes attached, and self-supervised training on unlabelled signal produces representations, not predictions. The scarce input is the join: continuous physiology from people who are not patients, tied to what eventually happens to them. Consent that reveals identity to no one. Nuraxi · SABA SABA 2.0: scaling to fifty thousand healthy humans, measured properly. The Sardinia Aging Biomarkers Analysis is our field study of healthy aging in one of the longest-lived populations on record. SABA 2.0 is now scaling to 50,000 participants, with continuous wearables joined to clinical events. At full scale, it becomes the largest dataset of healthy humans ever mapped. Why Sardinia The AKEA study documented centenarian prevalence of about 16.6 per 100,000 in the island's central-eastern highlands, against roughly 10 for Europe as a whole. Rarer still: the female advantage among centenarians, four or five to one worldwide, narrows to about two to one across the zone. It is a natural experiment with an unusually good archive, in a place where civil and parish records go back far enough to check the answer later. It is also home. Our founder grew up on the island and still has family there. Their grandparents died a good deal younger than their aunts and uncles are living, in the same villages, eating roughly the same food. That gap inside one family is the research question, and the second number is the harder half of it: the grandmother was ill for about two and a half years, the grandfather essentially not at all. What SABA measures People who are not ill, repeatedly, over time. The rarest data in medicine, and the half every clinical dataset is missing. Continuous physiology. Wearables on healthy adults, day and night, joined to blood biomarkers and clinical events as they happen. A verified baseline. First results, presented in Cagliari in December 2025 with our university partners: participants averaged 10,264 steps a day, 28% above UK Biobank and 47% above the US All of Us cohort. The objective function. SABA defines what exceptional aging looks like empirically, so models of health can be calibrated against people who aged well, not only against people who got sick. 50,000 Participants SABA 2.0 is scaling to, with wearables and clinical events 10,264 Steps per day averaged by participants in the first results Presented in Cagliari, December 2025 16.6 / 100k Centenarian prevalence in the Sardinian Blue Zone AKEA study, Experimental Gerontology, 2004 ≈ 2 : 1 Male-to-female centenarian ratio across the Sardinian Blue Zone, against four or five to one worldwide Poulain et al., Experimental Gerontology, 2004 Partners and funding SABA 1.0 , the 2025 prototype, was funded by Italy's PNRR through a cascade call at the University of Sassari , and by Nuraxi. SABA 2.0 is funded by Nuraxi. Not a government programme. A fuller account is coming. Run from Cagliari with Italian university partners. The Invisible Half | Nuraxi
Every model of human health is trained on people who were already sick, and the datasets with the most data have no idea what happened to anyone. An essay by Stefano Benedikter on informed presence bias, the healthspan gap, and what linkage buys.
Every model of human health is trained on people who were already sick. The models with the most data have no idea what happened to anyone.
The Invisible Half | Nuraxi Skip to content Demo Menu Home Solutions Use cases Research Request a demo Log in Portal Sign out Essay The Invisible Half Every model of human health is trained on people who were already sick. The models with the most data have no idea what happened to anyone. Stefano Benedikter Founder & CEO, Nuraxi 2026 24 minutes In 1943 the US Navy took a simple question to a group of statisticians working out of Columbia University. Bombers were coming back from raids over Europe full of holes. Where should the armour go? They had the data. Someone had mapped the bullet damage across every aircraft that returned: heavy concentration along the wings and the fuselage, very little around the engines and the cockpit. The answer looked obvious. Armour the wings. Abraham Wald told them to armour the engines. His reasoning took about a minute to state and a while to accept. The mapped planes were the ones that made it home. A hole in the wing was survivable, which is precisely why he was looking at so many of them. The engines showed clean not because they were never hit but because a plane hit there did not come back to be measured. The data was not describing where bombers got shot. It was describing where bombers could get shot and live. I have been thinking about Wald for two years, because every clinical dataset I have ever been offered has the same shape. And because the datasets that are supposed to fix that problem, the ones sitting on hundreds of millions of wrists, have a different flaw that almost nobody names. A single lifetime. Every dot is a moment the health system recorded something. Almost all of them fall after the first diagnosis. Part I: The record is a biased sample Sick patients have more data Here is the thing nobody says out loud when they pitch you a health data asset. A person appears in an electronic health record because something went wrong. That is the entry condition. Not birth, not residency, not age: a complaint serious enough to make somebody sit in a waiting room. Everything downstream of that moment gets captured in high resolution, and everything before it is dark. The informatics people worked this out a decade ago and named it. Weiskopf, Rusanov and Weng put it in a 2013 paper title with no ornament at all: sick patients have more data. Goldstein, Bhavsar, Phelan and Pencina called the underlying problem informed presence bias in the American Journal of Epidemiology in 2016, and theirs is the formulation that sticks. Inclusion in a health record is not random. It is itself a diagnosis of sorts. The sharpest demonstration came out of the BMJ in 2018. Denis Agniel, Isaac Kohane and Griffin Weber took 669,452 patients across two Boston hospitals and asked how well laboratory results predicted three-year survival. Then they asked the same question of the timing of those tests. Which day. What hour. How often the order was repeated. The timing frequently beat the result. Sit with that. The fact that a physician chose to draw blood at four in the morning carried more information about whether a patient would be alive in three years than what the blood actually contained. The record was describing the behaviour of a hospital at least as much as the biology of a human being. This is not a data quality problem in the ordinary sense. Nothing is missing, nothing is wrong, nobody made an error. The system is faithfully recording what it was built to record, which is illness at the moment of contact with a clinician. Build a model on it and you get a very good model of illness at the moment of contact with a clinician. I want that model. Nuraxi is building parts of it. But I have stopped pretending it is a model of health. Normal is a committee decision The gap shows up in something as ordinary as a blood panel. When a lab tells you a value is normal, it is comparing you against a reference interval. Under the standard the labs actually work to, that interval comes from a minimum of 120 reference individuals per partition, and it is drawn as the central 95 per cent of their distribution: everything between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentile. Two things follow, and both are uncomfortable. The first is arithmetic. If you take a perfectly healthy population and run enough panels, five per cent of those results come back flagged by construction. Not because anything is wrong. Because that is where the lines were drawn. The second is worse. Those 120 people are described in the literature as apparently healthy, which in practice has often meant blood donors, laboratory staff, or whoever was available and did not look unwell. The reference population for what counts as a normal human being is a convenience sample of people who happened to be standing near a phlebotomist. Then there is the individuality problem, which Eugene Harris laid out in Clinical Chemistry in 1974 and which has never been properly absorbed into practice. For most analytes, the variation within one person over time is much smaller than the variation between people. Your own personal range is narrow. The population range is wide. You can drift a long way from your own baseline, in a direction that means something, and never once leave the grey band on the printout. Nobody will call you. Nothing has happened, as far as the system is concerned. The healthy are invisible by construction The obvious rebuttal is that we do have data on well people. We have biobanks. Half a million volunteers in the UK alone. How that cohort was assembled is worth a minute. In 2017 Anna Fry and colleagues published the comparison in the American Journal of Epidemiology , and it is sobering. Roughly 9.2 million people were invited to join UK Biobank. About 5.4 per cent said yes. Those who said yes were not like those who did not. Less obesity, less smoking, less deprivation. At ages 70 to 74, all-cause mortality among participants ran 46.2 per cent lower in men and 55.5 per cent lower in women than in the general population. Total cancer incidence was 11.8 and 18.1 per cent lower. The best population health resource in the world is a sample of the unusually well, recruited by asking people whether they would like to spend a morning being measured. The people who never opened the letter are the ones nobody has looked at. This is Geoffrey Rose's argument, thirty years early and still unabsorbed. In 1985 he published “Sick individuals and sick populations” in the International Journal of Epidemiology , and his point was that the causes of individual cases and the causes of population incidence are different questions requiring different evidence. Study the ill and you learn about illness. You do not learn how the distribution of health is shaped, or what holds the bulk of a population on the healthy side of the line for decades at a time. So we have two problems stacked. The people in the clinical record are there because they are sick. The people in the research cohorts are there because they are well enough and interested enough to volunteer. Somewhere between those two is the actual population, and it is not well described by either. Part II: What it costs Where Medicine 3.0 stops Peter Attia has done more than anyone to move this conversation into public view, and the framing in Outlive is worth stating properly before taking issue with part of it. Medicine 1.0 was observation without mechanism. Medicine 2.0 is what we mostly have: germ theory, surgery, pharmacology, extraordinary at acute disease and largely reactive to chronic disease. Medicine 3.0 is his proposal for a practice that treats risk seriously decades ahead of diagnosis, that measures early, and that treats the marginal decade, the last ten years of function, as the thing actually being optimised. His image is the squared curve. Hold function high for as long as possible, then compress the decline into a short window at the end. The framing is right, and the field is slowly catching up to it. Here is my problem with the curve, and it is not a disagreement about direction. That curve is drawn with instruments from the diseased half. Every biomarker on an Attia-style panel exists because it was validated as a predictor of a disease, in a population selected for having or developing that disease. ApoB matters because of what it does to arteries in people whose arteries failed. The clocks, the panels, the imaging: all of them are calibrated against pathology, then run in reverse and pointed at people who feel fine. That is a legitimate and useful move. It is also a borrowed map. We are using the topography of decline to infer the topography of flourishing, and assuming the second is just the first with the sign flipped. It is not. Staying well for forty years is not the arithmetic negative of getting sick. It has its own dynamics, its own variance, its own signatures, and we have barely looked at them because the people doing it well are not in any database. Curve form after Attia. The shading is mine: clinical data is generated on the descent, and the plateau is inferred rather than observed. Nine point six years Now the number that made me rebuild the company's thesis. In 2024 Armin Garmany and Andre Terzic published an analysis in JAMA Network Open covering 183 WHO member states. They measured the distance between living and living well. The global mean was 9.6 years. For the United States it was 12.4, the widest gap in the world. Women's gap ran 2.4 years wider than men's. And the gap has been growing, not shrinking, across the two decades they examined. The WHO's own 2021 numbers agree. Global life expectancy 71.4 years against healthy life expectancy of 61.9. Japan, the longevity exemplar, lives 84.5 years and lives well for 73.4. Italy 82.2 against 70.6. The United States 76.4 against 63.9, which puts American healthy life expectancy below China's. Every one of those gaps is a decade. A tenth of a life, or more, spent inside a body that is failing in ways somebody is managing rather than fixing. James Fries predicted the opposite. His 1980 paper in the New England Journal of Medicine proposed the compression of morbidity: as we got better at prevention, the sick period at the end of life would shrink toward a short, sharp decline. It was a beautiful hypothesis and forty years of data have not been kind to it. We added years to life. We added at least as many to the period of illness. I am not neutral about this. It is the central failure of twentieth century medicine, and it is a measurement failure before it is a treatment failure. You cannot compress what you do not count. WHO Global Health Observatory, 2021. Every gap is longer than a decade. A name for the second number Which brings me to the thing I actually want to propose. We have a word for the good part. Healthspan: the years lived in function. It is in every deck in the longevity sector and it has done real work in shifting how people think. We have no equivalent word for the other part, at the level of an individual person, stated forward in time. There should be one, because the sector optimises what it names. Morbispan. The expected number of years a person will live carrying one or more chronic conditions. Not a population statistic. A personal one, predicted, with a confidence interval, updated as you live. Your healthspan is 71 years and your morbispan is 14. Here is what moves the second number. Let me be honest about the prior art, because this is a crowded conceptual space and I would rather say so than get corrected. The WHO's healthy life expectancy already measures something close, at national level. So does disability-free life expectancy. So do the Global Burden of Disease measures, years lived with disability and disability-adjusted life years, which the IHME has refined for three decades. Eurostat publishes Healthy Life Years for every member state. All of them are population averages, computed backward from mortality tables and prevalence surveys. None of them tells a specific forty-two year old how many years of chronic illness sit in front of her, or what would change that. The second number has no name at the level of a person. I am proposing one. Part III: Two half-blind datasets The dark matter of health Finding the right way to describe this took a while, and the first metaphor was the wrong one. The obvious one is yin and yang: disease on one side, health on the other. It does not survive contact with the source. In Chinese medicine health is the dynamic balance of yin and yang, and disease is the imbalance between them. Neither pole is the sick one. The popular Western reading, two opposed forces with values attached, inverts the original. I dropped it. The one that holds is dark matter. Roughly 85 per cent of the matter in the universe has never been directly observed. We know it is there from what it does to the things we can see: galaxies rotate faster than their visible mass allows, light bends around apparently empty space. Four decades of increasingly sensitive detectors, some of them a kilometre underground, have not caught a single particle of it. Cosmology did not respond to this by declaring the visible 15 per cent to be the universe. It built the standard model around the missing majority and went looking. Medicine did the opposite. We built the model out of the visible fraction, called it human health, and stopped. Every model of health is trained on the sick half The last three years have produced the first real foundation models of human health, and they are genuinely impressive pieces of work. Delphi-2M came out in Nature in September 2025, from teams at EMBL-EBI, the DKFZ and Copenhagen. It is a modified GPT architecture trained on around 400,000 UK Biobank participants, predicting rates for more than a thousand diseases plus mortality, and it was validated without retraining against roughly 1.9 million people in the Danish national registries. Average area under the curve of about 0.76 internally, 0.67 on external validation. It generates synthetic disease trajectories up to twenty years forward. All of that from a model of around 2.2 million parameters, which should embarrass anyone who thinks scale is the only lever. Foresight, published in The Lancet Digital Health in 2024 by Zeljko Kraljevic, Richard Dobson and colleagues, applies the same generative logic to hospital records: given a patient's history of disorders, medications and procedures, what comes next. Zeljko built that at King's College London before he joined me, and he is now our chief scientist. life2vec, in Nature Computational Science in 2024, ran the same idea across Danish life-event data. Now look at what every one of them was trained on. Registries. Claims. Hospital records. Biobank participants recruited by letter. The diseased half, in every case. Not by oversight but because that is the data that exists at scale. We are training Wald's Navy. Armour the wings, with transformers. The other failure: volume without labels The obvious answer is wearables, and this is where care is needed, because the wearable story is usually told wrong. Start with the volume, which is genuinely staggering. A consumer wrist device runs photoplethysmography at somewhere between 25 and 100 hertz. At 25 hertz that is roughly 2.2 million samples a day from a single optical channel. Add three-axis accelerometry at comparable rates and you are into tens of millions of raw samples per person per day. Google's own published work notes that a sensor at 100 hertz produces on the order of 17 million time points per day, which is why the industry stores minute-level summaries rather than raw waveforms. Per person, per month, that is tens of millions to billions of samples. Against a few dozen structured observations a year from the clinic. The asymmetry is not a factor of ten. It is a factor of a million. Our own materials have carried a figure of 1.2 million data points per user per month. That is low by two to three orders of magnitude and I am correcting it here rather than quietly. The model builders have moved on this. In 2025 Apple published a wearable behaviour model trained on roughly 2.5 billion hours of data from about 162,000 participants in its Heart and Movement Study. Google went further: SensorFM, published in 2026, was pretrained on more than a trillion minutes of sensor data from around five million consented Fitbit and Pixel Watch users across a hundred countries. Google's earlier scaling work found something that should give any builder pause: total hours of data mattered more than the number of distinct people. These are enormous, serious models. And here is the part that took me a while to see clearly. They do not know what happened to anyone. A wearable records physiology continuously and outcomes never. It does not know that the person wearing it was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation in March, started metformin in June, was admitted in November, or died. It sees the signal and none of the story. The data is unlabelled. Self-supervised pretraining on an unlabelled signal produces representations of that signal, which is a real achievement and is not the same thing as a prediction. Turning a representation into a clinical forecast requires labelled outcomes, and the labels are exactly what the wrist cannot supply. The published work says this plainly if you read the methods. Apple's behaviour model was evaluated against health states derived from surveys and HealthKit entries, not adjudicated diagnoses. Google's PH-LLM, in Nature Medicine in 2025, predicted self-reported sleep quality and gave coaching, and its authors were explicit that this is not clinical diagnosis. The UK Biobank self-supervised activity work in npj Digital Medicine in 2024 describes pretraining as reducing the need for labelled data. Reducing. Not removing. Even the famous screening trials hit the same wall. The Apple Heart Study enrolled 419,297 people and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2019. Outcomes were not established by looking at anyone's medical record. They came from a telehealth visit and a mailed ECG patch, and the authors stated their own limitation clearly: the pragmatic design meant outcomes were reported by participants, which limited the ability to confirm the diagnosis. Of 419,297 participants, roughly 450 ECG patches were analysable. The Fitbit Heart Study, 455,699 participants, worked the same way and returned about a thousand usable patches. Half a million people. A thousand confirmed answers. The clinical record knows what happened and almost nothing about the body in between. The wearable knows the body continuously and nothing about what happened. The Apple point, stated precisely It is tempting to say Apple and Google are sitting on the answer and have not bothered to join it up. That is not quite right, and the real version is more interesting. Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices on its January 2026 earnings call. But Apple's Health data is end-to-end encrypted, and Apple's own security documentation states that it is not readable by anyone, Apple included. With Advanced Data Protection switched on, the keys sit in the user's keychain and Apple cannot produce the data under legal process either. So Apple's position is not that it holds the world's largest health dataset and has failed to link it. Apple's position is that, by architectural choice, it cannot see one. What Apple can see is what people explicitly donate through the Research app, which is how the Heart and Movement Study reached its 278,000 participants. That is a research cohort, not an install base. Google's constraint is legal rather than cryptographic. When the European Commission cleared the Fitbit acquisition in December 2020, it did so subject to ten years of commitments: no Fitbit health data in Google Ads across the EEA, a technical silo separating health data from advertising data, continued free access to the Fitbit web API, and a real user choice about whether other Google services touch the health data. The theory of harm was advertising, so research use is not barred. But the silo is real. This deserves fairness, because it is the kind of claim a company can correct in public. Neither firm is negligent, and both have built something genuinely hard. What neither has, and what nobody has at consumer scale, is continuous physiology joined to adjudicated clinical outcomes for millions of people. What linkage actually buys The proof that this is the binding constraint arrived in January 2026, in Nature Medicine . A Stanford group took a sleep foundation model, the kind pretrained self-supervised on raw polysomnography, and did the one thing the wearable field has not managed. They linked roughly 35,000 sleep studies to as much as 25 years of electronic health record diagnosis codes, and fine-tuned with a survival objective. The same architecture that had previously done signal classification started predicting 130 different conditions. Mortality at a concordance index of 0.84. Dementia at 0.85. Nothing changed about the sensor data. What changed is that the model was finally told what happened to the people. The other demonstration is the NIH's All of Us programme. Its latest release holds Fitbit data from more than 59,000 participants spanning fourteen years, 39 million step observations and 31 million sleep observations, and roughly 46 per cent of those participants also contributed electronic health records, genomics and surveys. The landmark analysis, Master and colleagues in Nature Medicine in 2022, could only assemble 6,042 people who had both consented to share their records and worn a Fitbit for at least six months. From those 6,042, across 5.9 million person-days, they showed that an increase of 2,000 daily steps was associated with lower incidence of type 2 diabetes, obesity and major depressive disorder. Six thousand people produced that finding. Not six million. From half a billion wrists to a few thousand people whose sensor data is joined to a clinical record. Run the funnel and the scarcity is obvious. Something over 560 million smartwatch users worldwide as of 2025. Fifty-nine thousand in the best-linked public research cohort on earth. Twenty-seven thousand of those with records attached. Six thousand in the study that actually produced the result. That collapse, from hundreds of millions to thousands, is the whole opportunity. Part IV: Why nobody has done it The barriers are not technical, which is what makes them tractable. In the United States, consumer wearable data mostly falls outside HIPAA, because the company holding it is usually neither a covered entity nor a business associate. The Federal Trade Commission fills part of the gap through its Health Breach Notification Rule, and states like Washington have legislated their own versions. The result is a patchwork in which the clinical record is heavily regulated, the wearable stream is lightly regulated, and joining them crosses a legal boundary nobody designed on purpose. In Europe the picture is changing fast. Health data sits in the special category under Article 9 of the GDPR, prohibited by default and permitted only through explicit consent or a research exemption. On top of that, the European Health Data Space Regulation entered into force in March 2025, with secondary-use provisions phasing in toward 2029, and it declined to exclude wellness-application data from its scope. The EU Data Act has applied since September 2025 and gives people rights over data generated by connected products, wearables included. Read those together and Europe is building, slowly and with characteristic complexity, exactly the legal rails this work requires. The remaining problem is identity. Joining a wrist to a record without either holder learning who the person is has a known solution in outline: privacy-preserving record linkage using one-way hashed tokens is already in production across US research networks, matching millions of patients across datasets under the HIPAA expert determination standard. The techniques exist. Almost nobody has pointed them at consumer sensor data. Part V: Ogliastra Which is why I keep going back to a stretch of mountain in the middle of Sardinia. In 2004 Michel Poulain, Giovanni Pes and colleagues published the AKEA study in Experimental Gerontology . Working through parish and civil records in the central-eastern highlands, around Nuoro and Ogliastra, they found centenarian prevalence of about 16.6 per 100,000 against roughly 10.0 for Europe as a whole. The prevalence was interesting. The sex ratio was the finding. Almost everywhere on earth, centenarians are women by a margin of four or five to one. Across this zone the ratio was close to two to one, and in Villagrande Strisaili, documented by Poulain, Pes and Luisa Salaris in the Journal of Aging Research in 2011, men reached a hundred about as often as women. The female advantage in longevity, one of the most stable findings in all of demography, is not there. I grew up on that island and my family is still there. My grandparents died a good deal younger than my aunts and uncles are living, in the same villages, eating roughly the same food, and that gap inside one family is the question I keep coming back to. The part that took me longer to see is the second number. My grandmother was ill for about two and a half years. My grandfather, essentially not at all. Their lives were shorter and their morbispan was close to nothing, which is the outcome this whole essay argues for, arrived at by accident and measured by nobody. The island is not a magic trick. It is a natural experiment with an unusually good archive. Now the part most people in this sector skip, and I am not going to. Saul Newman won the Ig Nobel Prize in Demography in September 2024 for showing that supercentenarian records track poverty, missing birth certificates and bad record-keeping more tightly than they track health. His figures are hard to wave away. Roughly 18 per cent of so-called validated supercentenarians have a birth certificate. The introduction of state birth registration is associated with a 69 to 82 per cent drop in supercentenarian records. In 1997 the Italian state discovered around 30,000 dead people still drawing pensions. His central papers remain preprints, and his critique lands hardest on aggregate records rather than individually validated cases, which is a real distinction. But anyone selling Blue Zone data who has not read him is either uninformed or hoping you have not. Here is what I take from it. Newman does not weaken the argument. He strengthens it. If our records of the exceptionally long-lived are that fragile, the case for going and measuring properly, prospectively, with instruments rather than parish ledgers, is stronger than it was before he published. That is what SABA is for. The Sardinian Aging Biomarkers Analysis is a field study of aging biomarkers and mechanisms of resilience in one of the longest-lived populations on record, with Ugo Faraguna of the University of Pisa as principal investigator. The 2025 prototype was funded through Italy's PNRR programme, via the University of Sassari, and by us. The study now running is funded by Nuraxi. I would rather say that plainly than let a national programme stand in for our own commitment. The reason SABA matters to a model is not that Sardinians are exotic. It is that the study measures people who are not ill, repeatedly, over time, in a place where the archive goes back far enough to check the answer later. That is the rarest data in medicine. What it costs to keep not knowing Andrew Scott, Martin Ellison and David Sinclair published the estimate in Nature Aging in 2021. One added year of healthy life expectancy, valued across the whole population, comes to about 38 trillion dollars. Ten years, 367 trillion. Their more interesting finding, and the one relevant here, is that improvements which compress morbidity are worth more than improvements that simply extend life. The compression is worth more than the extension, and the compression is the thing we have never measured. Li et al., BMJ 2020. Five crude factors buy a woman ten disease-free years. There is evidence the lever exists, even measured crudely. Yanping Li and colleagues in the BMJ in 2020 looked at life expectancy free of diabetes, cardiovascular disease and cancer at age 50. Women with none of five low-risk lifestyle factors: 23.7 disease-free years. Women with four or five: 34.4. For men, 23.5 against 31.1. Ten years of disease-free life for women. Seven and a half for men. From five factors so blunt they fit on a napkin: not smoking, a body mass index between 18.5 and 24.9, half an hour of activity a day, moderate alcohol, a diet in the top 40 per cent. If crude instruments buy a decade, I want to know what precise ones buy. Nobody can tell me, because the measurement has never been done on the people who are not sick. What we are building Two halves, joined. The first half is the one the field already works on: disease trajectories learned from clinical records, at scale, with the generative architectures Foresight and Delphi-2M have shown work. We are not abandoning that. It is real and it saves lives. The second half is continuous physiology from people who are not patients. Not because the signal beats a lab panel, but because it is the only instrument that observes the forty years nobody watches. The part that matters is the join. A wearable stream with an outcome attached is worth more than a thousand streams without one, and the Stanford sleep result is the cleanest published evidence of it. Our work in Sardinia is designed around it: measure people who are not ill, repeatedly, in a population where the clinical record and the civil archive both go back far enough to tell you later what happened. The consent architecture is the hard engineering problem, and we treat it as one rather than as a compliance afterthought. Blind tokenisation lets a person's sensor stream and their clinical record be matched without either holder learning who the person is. The technical bet is that a model trained on both halves learns something neither half contains. Where the boundary actually sits. What the last quiet years before a diagnosis look like from the inside. Whether the thing we call the onset of disease is a threshold crossing, or the visible part of a slope that started decades earlier. My read is that it is the slope, and that we have been treating an arbitrary point on it as an event because that is where the billing code fires. The call Here is the position, dated and falsifiable. I think that within five years the leading models of human health will be trained on continuous physiology joined to clinical outcomes, and that organisations holding only one side will find themselves where Wald's Navy was: enormous quantities of data, meticulously collected, describing survivable damage. The winner will not be whoever has the most sensor hours. Google already has a trillion minutes and it has not made anyone healthier yet. It will be whoever solves consent and linkage first, because that is the scarce input and everything else is downstream of it. And morbispan, or whatever the field ends up calling it, becomes a number people know about themselves the way they know their cholesterol. We are trying to be that group. Sardinia is where we started, because it is where my family is from and because the natural experiment is genuinely rare. If you think I have the direction wrong, I would like to hear it. And if you are sitting on continuous physiological data with outcomes attached, which almost nobody is, that is the conversation I most want to have this year.
